source_document.body:
With the possibility of the New York City Delivery Protection Act headed toward some sort of amended structure and then a vote in the New York City Council before the end of the year, the push against it has ramped into high gear.
The opponents who have become increasingly visible just in the past few weeks–it’s tough to watch television in New York these days and after a little while not see one of their ads –have held onsite rallies and found an active media voice writing on the issue in a mostly critical way in The New York Post.
Its latest article cites Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) warnings that the Act, if passed as is, could add $5 to every package it delivers in the city.
That brought a retort on X from Council Speaker Julie Menin, whose views on how the final version of the Act will look are considered vital to its outcome,
It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections. We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs. If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6 — Speaker Julie Menin (@SpeakerMenin) November 19, 2026
The battle at times is taking on unusual political positioning. If it is assumed that the main target of the bill is Amazon–even though other companies like FedEx (NYSE: FDX) will be greatly affected as well–some of the arguments being made against the bill by the collection of direct service providers operating under the banner of the New York Delivers Coalition are muddying a traditional left/right dichotomy.
Amazon has long been a target of politicians on the left. Sen. Bernie Sanders has ripped the company’s “corporate greed.” Former vice president and Democratic Presidential candidate Kamala Harris suggested Amazon and other big tech companies should be regulated . And Democratic Socialist Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was seen as a key reason in her first term why Amazon pulled out of its plans to build an East Coast headquarters in New York City, having led the opposition to the plan (with Amazon eventually choosing northern Virginia as its site.)
That hasn’t changed in New York City, with Democratic Socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani actively backing the Delivery Protection Act.
Not normally heard from Amazon backers
In the last two weeks, New York Delivers has staged a demonstration on the steps of New York City Hall and were planning Thursday to protest at the district headquarters of Tiffany Caban, the member of the Council who introduced the Delivery Protection Act last year.
But this stepped-up opposition is coming with actions and statements that seem more out of a New York demonstration from the left than actions that implicitly could be seen as supporting Amazon, a corporation long vilified by the left.
For example, at the City Hall rally, one of the speakers commenced the chant of “No Justice, No Peace!” which has long been identified as the protest motto of The Rev. Al Sharpton.
And at the latest public media conference , ostensibly called to discuss the legal issues with the Delivery Protection Act seen by its opponents, the issue of race came up repeatedly and dominated the discussion far more than possible litigation. It echoed similar statements from the November 12 rally at City Hall.
“The Council should consider the burden that this legislation would place on business owners as well as their employees,” Derek Sells, chairman of the Cochran Law Firm that is the outside counsel to New York Delivers, told the gathering.
But he then raised a racial aspect of the bill.
Racial makeup at the DSPs
Sells cited research by AKRF, a consulting firm, that said “80% of last mile delivery workers are people of color, 88% live in New York City, and 49% live in state-designated disadvantaged communities,” Sells said.
The study estimates that between 3,000 and more than 10,000 workers could lose their jobs, according to Sells.
Mark Morial, the former mayor of New Orleans and now the CEO of the National Urban League, said at the media conference that “it was puzzling to me why a city that considers itself in the progressive mode would even see legislation like this as helping workers. In fact, it would destroy the businesses owned by the people standing with me, as well as many others, with no guarantee for their workers, with no compensation for their losses.”
That sort of discussion took up most of the roughly half-hour session with specifics on the legal issues few and far between.
Laying it out in a letter
But it was in a nine-page letter to Speaker Menin that the law-based arguments were explored in greater depth.
The core of the Delivery Protection Act is that one, delivery companies in New York City would need a license to operate; two, those companies can not hire subcontractors; three, the delivery companies would be required to hire any workers displaced by the end to subcontracting; and four, the licenses can be yanked for violation of any number of rules.
It is projected that if the bill is adopted with its original wording (though an overhaul of the language is expected), it would require Amazon to purchase its roughly 100 DSPs operating in the city because of the no subcontracting rule and turn their workers into employees of Amazon rather than their current DSP.
The Teamsters have strongly backed the Delivery Protection Act. The union has sought to unionize direct employees of Amazon, with a recent success in Canada and a long frustrating battle elsewhere in New York City.
To unionize the DSP drivers has been an even tougher challenge.
Sells’ letter cites three broad areas where he thinks the Delivery Protection Act is legally problematic.
First, “Federal law limits the ability of cities and states to dictate how delivery companies operate, including how they organize their delivery services and who performs the work,” Sells’ letter says.
Second, the law also conflicts with New York code, according to Sells. “New York State already has laws that determine when delivery drivers must be classified as employees and when companies can legally use independent businesses to perform delivery work. Intro 518 (another term for the Delivery Protection Act) would prohibit business arrangements that state law already allows and regulates,” Sells writes.
The third point, Sells said, is that the city can not override either federal or state law.
“Intro 518 also appears to reach drivers and businesses operating outside the five boroughs, including facilities in New Jersey, Westchester, and Long Island,” Sells’ letter says. “This raises additional legal questions about the City’s authority to regulate businesses beyond its borders and its impact on interstate commerce.”
The Sells letter also gets into some of the same issues heard from the steps of City Hall: the racial makeup of the DSP work force as well as the company owners, issues that may have political heft but are questionable as legal matters.
But where Sells ties them together is arguing that lawsuits that would follow the introduction of the Delivery Protection Act could drag on a long time, and it would be people of color most affected by that uncertainty.
The law, “if enacted, would invite years of costly litigation with a substantial risk that the Act’s core would be struck down, leaving workers without the protections the Council intends while the small businesses that employ them close in the interim,” the Sells letter said. “Those harms would fall most heavily on Black, Latino, immigrant, and outer-borough New Yorkers.”
F4A makes an appearance
One of the legal arguments raised by Sells is that the Delivery Protection Act could be in conflict with the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act (F4A).
That law has the well-known provision that states are barred from taking action that could impact a “price, route or service.”
It had been at the core of the now-settled legal dispute over California’s AB5 independent contractor law, and more recently was tossed out as a shield against broker liability in the case of Montgomery vs. Caribe Transport II.
Sells cited federal precedents that found laws Sells views as similar to the Delivery Protection Act regarding independent contractor status or hiring requirements were in violation of F4A.
Sells says the Delivery Protection Act “goes further” than the laws that were the subject of the earlier precedents cited in his letter.
Sells’ letter said he “anticipates” that the Act’s backers might turn to the safety exception of F4A to thwart the proposed law from overriding the act in its entirety. The safety exception allows state action like a tort in an action that might otherwise be seen as impacting a “price, route or service.”
“Anticipating” that the backers of the Act might counter with the safety exception–which applies to motor vehicles–as providing justification for the Act despite the rest of F4A, Sells says “a rule dictating the corporate identity of a driver’s employer, and banning an entire category of business relationship, regulates business structure, not vehicles.”

The forward radar on 6,185 Kenworth and Peterbilt trucks built between Feb. 11 and Oct. 8 can trigger braking for stopped or slow-moving vehicles in the left lane. PACCAR disclosed the defect in a Nov. 11 recall filing with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.
Kenworth T680 and Peterbilt 579 tractors make up 5,498 of the trucks, all model year 2027. The recall is at least the fifth PACCAR has filed on 2027 trucks since July, NHTSA records show. One covered 5,919 trucks whose power distribution box may cont a in oil .
As of Nov. 4, PACCAR had received eight warranty claims and eight field reports that may be related to the radar defect. No deaths or injuries have been reported. The company estimates 0.1% of the recalled trucks have the defect.
“Forward collision mitigation is not affected because camera functionality detects objects in the same lane of travel,” PACCAR wrote in the filing. It lists no warning to the driver before a false braking event, and it does not advise owners to stop driving the trucks.
Cause traced to radar parameter data
The filing traces the cause to a parameter calculator PACCAR uses. The calculator produces a software data set that is not written correctly into the radar’s memory.
When the radar does not learn the truck’s specific parameters, it defaults to a lateral position too far left of its true position, PACCAR told NHTSA. The radar can then track stationary or slow-moving objects in the left lane as “relevant objects.”
Timeline from complaints to recall
PACCAR’s safety and compliance team learned of field complaints about automatic emergency braking events on Oct. 16 and held trucks at its plants, according to the filing’s chronology. Corrected software was available on Oct. 19 for trucks still at the plants and in production.
On Oct. 20 and again on Oct. 30, PACCAR spoke with Bendix, the radar’s supplier, about the radar parameter issue. Its safety committee decided Nov. 4 to recall the trucks. The recall count is based on the radar part numbers and quantities Bendix shipped to PACCAR, minus trucks corrected at the plants.
Heavy-truck emergency braking rule still pending
NHTSA and the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration proposed in June 2023 to require automatic emergency braking on new trucks over 10,000 pounds. Three weeks earlier, NHTSA had opened a preliminary evaluation of about 250,000 Freightliner Cascadias after 18 owner complaints that the system braked with no hazard present.
In 2025, the agencies moved the rule back to the proposal stage . The Transportation Department’s regulatory agenda targeted July 2026 for a supplemental proposal, which has not been published.
Software fix and owner letters
The remedy is a field software update that corrects the radar memory issue, according to the filing. PACCAR plans to notify dealers and owners on Jan. 10, 2027, the same day the trucks’ VINs become searchable on NHTSA’s recall lookup . Peterbilt owners can call 940-591-4220 and Kenworth owners 425-828-5888 about recall 26PACL.
Why it matters: Fleet managers running 2027 Kenworth or Peterbilt tractors built since February may want to brief drivers on unintended braking near slow left-lane traffic until the software update is done. VIN lookups open Jan. 10, 2027, when fleets can confirm which units need the update.

Ministro Hales plant. ( Image: Codelco | Flickr. )
Posted By: Cecilia Jamasmie November 19, 2026
Chile’s environmental regulator has accused state-owned copper producer Codelco of two serious dust-control violations at its Ministro Hales mine, exposing the operation to fines, closure or the loss of its environmental permit.
The Superintendencia del Medio Ambiente (SMA) announced the charges Thursday following inspections and seven public complaints submitted between 2021 and 2024 in Calama, a northern Chilean city designated as exceeding legal limits for inhalable particulate pollution. Each charge carries a maximum fine of 5,000 annual tax units, equivalent to about $4.3 million (C$6.2 million), for combined potential fines of $8.7 million.
“Calama is an area declared saturated with respirable particulate matter, so strict compliance with emissions-control measures is essential to protect public health,” environmental superintendent Emanuel Ibarra said in a Spanish-language statement.
The enforcement action follows environmental approval in January for a $2.8-billion project to extend Ministro Hales’ operating life to 2054. Codelco said the expansion would lift annual copper output to about 200,000 tonnes from roughly 170,000 tonnes.
Dust control failures
The SMA alleges that Codelco operated the mine’s primary crusher without the baghouse filtration system required under its environmental approvals. The regulator also alleges that dust-removal efficiency fell below the mandated 75% between November 2023 and February 2024.
A second charge concerns Codelco’s alleged failure to apply bischofite, a magnesium chloride-based dust suppressant, to inactive areas of its waste-rock dump during 2023 and 2024. The treatment was intended to reduce wind erosion by 85%.
That charge also cites missing records documenting implementation of the dust-control measures between 2023 and 2025.
Both alleged breaches were classified as serious under Chilean environmental law. The charges are not final findings of wrongdoing, and any sanctions will depend on the outcome of the proceedings.
Tailings compliance
In a separate decision, the SMA approved a compliance program submitted by Codelco to address groundwater infiltration and tailings-management violations at the Talabre tailings facility.
The regulator had filed charges in August 2024 after finding that the company failed to implement a contingency plan in response to changes in groundwater conditions and deposited tailings with a solids content below the required 60%.
The approved program includes eight measures to be implemented over 24 months at an estimated cost of 66.9 billion Chilean pesos ($66.8 million).
Among the main commitments, Codelco will install 22 additional extraction wells to strengthen the facility’s hydraulic containment barrier, which is monitored through 17 wells.
The company will also implement its PRECLA tailings preclassification project to achieve the required solids concentration and conduct water-capture tests within the tailings basin.
Approval of the program suspends the earlier enforcement proceedings while Codelco carries out the agreed measures. If the company fails to meet its commitments, the SMA can reopen the case and impose fines of up to twice those otherwise applicable to the original violations. Print

source_document.body:
Swedish advanced nuclear developer Blykalla has signed an agreement with Urenco that the companies describe as the world’s first high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) enrichment contract for a commercial lead-cooled reactor. The agreement covers Blykalla’s first commercial 55-MWe Swedish Advanced Lead Reactor (SEALER), which the company plans to deploy in the U.S.
The agreement, signed Nov. 12 at Urenco’s London headquarters and announced Nov. 16 , calls for Blykalla to supply the uranium feed and Urenco to enrich the material at its Advanced Fuels Facility in Capenhurst, England. Urenco plans to bring the facility online in 2031 and begin deliveries to Blykalla in the early 2030s.
“We expect to be able to announce more about the location and schedule in the near future,” Blykalla CEO Jacob Stedman said in written responses to POWER .
“Deliveries under the Urenco contract are planned to begin when Capenhurst comes online in the early 2030s, which aligns with the schedule for our first commercial reactor,” he said. “Blykalla holds one of the first contracts on what is set to be one of the first commercial HALEU facilities in the West.”
Neither company disclosed the contract value or the enrichment level specified for the SEALER fuel.
“The quantities under this contract are confidential, but we can confirm that the agreement secures HALEU enrichment for at least our first commercial unit,” Stedman said. “It is a concrete step in executing our fuel supply strategy and provides a foundation for our broader deployment plans.”
Urenco Builds Commercial HALEU Enrichment Capacity
The agreement is Urenco’s third HALEU supply contract. In September 2025, the enrichment company signed an agreement covering Radiant’s Kaleidos microreactor , which Urenco described as the first binding commercial contract by a U.S. advanced reactor developer for Western HALEU enrichment services. A subsequent agreement with Antares Nuclear in May 2026 established a multi-year HALEU supply arrangement.
A February 2026 statement from the U.K. government identified Russia as the world’s only commercial source of HALEU . The U.S. and U.K. are pursuing domestic enrichment capabilities to address anticipated demand from advanced reactor developers and reduce dependence on Russian nuclear fuel supplies. The U.S. ban on imports of Russian low-enriched uranium took effect Aug. 11, 2024, subject to temporary waivers.
The Department of Energy (DOE) defines HALEU as uranium enriched above 5% but below 20% uranium-235, compared to enrichment levels of up to 5% for fuel typically used in the existing commercial reactor fleet. Higher enrichment levels can enable more compact reactor cores, longer operating cycles, and improved fuel utilization. The agency has projected that domestic HALEU demand could reach 50 metric tons annually by 2035 .
In May 2024, the U.K. government awarded Urenco £196 million under a program that commits up to £300 million to establish a domestic HALEU supply chain. The Capenhurst facility represents a total investment of approximately £400 million, including Urenco’s contribution. Urenco has outlined an initial production capacity of up to 27 metric tons of HALEU annually and designed the facility to accommodate future expansion.
Blykalla’s Uranium Dioxide Fuel Supply Strategy
The Urenco agreement, notably, covers only the enrichment stage of the nuclear fuel cycle. Blykalla has not identified the suppliers that will provide the finished fuel for its first commercial reactor. “We are developing an integrated sourcing strategy across procurement, conversion, deconversion, and fuel fabrication,” Stedman noted. “The Urenco agreement establishes a clear basis for this work, since it defines the enrichment quantities and delivery schedule around which we can coordinate the other supply chain steps for our first reactor. It also helps define our fuel fabrication requirements, an area where further investment is needed in both the US and Europe.”
Blykalla’s SEALER is a compact, lead-cooled fast reactor designed for factory production and road transport. The small modular reactor (SMR) incorporates the company’s proprietary aluminum-alloyed steel, developed to resist corrosion associated with liquid lead. Lead’s high boiling point allows the coolant to operate at atmospheric pressure, while natural circulation enables residual heat removal without pumps. The company also cites lead’s capacity to retain radioactive iodine and provide gamma radiation shielding as safety attributes.
Blykalla’s SEALER advanced modular reactor uses lead-cooled fast reactor technology developed over 25 years of research at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. The company filed its first commercial application for a six-unit, 330-MWe SEALER park at Norrsundet, Sweden, in May 2026. Courtesy: Blykalla
Stedman confirmed that Blykalla has selected uranium dioxide (UO ₂ )—the predominant fuel material in the existing commercial nuclear reactor fleet—for its SEALER design. “Our choice of uranium dioxide fuel allows us to build on decades of qualification experience and industrial production,” Stedman said. “This provides a strong foundation for fuel development and procurement, with opportunities to draw on capabilities in the light water reactor industry. Our fuel will require qualification for Blykalla’s specific operating conditions, but that established experience can support a faster path to deployment.”
Blykalla Advances U.S. and Swedish Reactor Development
Blykalla’s U.S. development program encompasses Fjäll, its first-of-a-kind nuclear demonstration reactor, and the SEALER-55 for commercial deployment. The company initiated pre-application engagement with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) in June 2026 but has not yet filed a license application.
In September, Blykalla opened a technical center in Austin, Texas , to accommodate engineering and reactor development teams. The company also announced a collaboration with Microsoft to incorporate artificial intelligence (AI) tools into its regulatory documentation and licensing processes.
Blykalla has also established a strategic partnership with U.S. sodium-cooled fast reactor developer Oklo. Oklo, Norrsken Launcher, and Armada Investment co-led Blykalla’s $50 million funding round in December 2025 . In March 2026, the companies expanded their collaboration to encompass technical work on Oklo’s DOE-authorized reactor pilot project and potential fast-neutron irradiation testing in Oklo powerhouses. Blykalla outlined prospective U.S. commitments of $100 million to $200 million and the involvement of 30 to 40 engineers, subject to final planning and approvals.
In Sweden, Blykalla and Uniper are developing SEALER-E, an electric prototype at the OKG nuclear power plant in Oskarshamn. The company is also pursuing two commercial reactor parks that could accommodate a combined 14 SEALER units.
In May, Blykalla submitted an application to the Swedish government for a six-unit, 330-MW reactor park at Norrsundet in Gävle municipality. In August, it submitted a second application for up to eight units totaling 440 MW at Untra in Tierp municipality. Blykalla targets initial operations at Untra in the first half of the 2030s, contingent on approvals from the Swedish government, regulatory agencies, courts, and Tierp municipality.
“We are coordinating our commercialization efforts in Sweden and the US through a common supply chain strategy,” Stedman told POWER . “We are executing that strategy by securing contracts that give suppliers the demand visibility and commitments they need to invest in additional fuel cycle capacity. Across the two markets, we see opportunities to share fuel suppliers, manufacturing capabilities, and technology qualification work where technical and regulatory requirements allow. Investment in both U.S. and European supply chains will be essential to support our deployment plans and to meet broader SMR demand.”
— Sonal C. Patel is a POWER senior editor ( @sonalcpatel , @POWERmagazine ).

For Couples: Forest River Shows Off They Can Be a Serious RV Brand With 2027 Pause Reboot 14.3
15 photos
Photo: Forest River Inc
Usually, when you do out there and lock your eyes onto a compact travel trailer, you expect to also come across an equally ‘compact’ price. Well, when we’re talking about Forest River’s Pause Reboot 14.3, the idea that a smaller camper is accompanied by a small price goes out the window.
That’s because, for the time being, a 2027 Pause Reboot 14.3 is currently selling in select dealerships for an average of $75,000, a price that usually lands you in a massive travel trailer suitable for an entire family, and not just a traveling couple. Why is that? That’s what we’re here to find out.
If you’ve ever followed along with content revolving around this camper , you’re aware that this one is nothing like your average travel trailer of this size. Since it was launched in 2024, people have even come to love the Pause Reboot class for its ability to be a dependable solution for off-grid camping.
Photo: Forest River Inc Now, there are countless ways to build a camper, and at the core of the 14.3, Forest River ditched the wood and calls upon a completely composite and aluminum-framed design. This means a camper that’s as impervious to the elements as possible and one that is also as light as can be.
The latter is relative to just how capable a camper may be, and in the case of the 14.3, keep in mind that it weighs 4,583 lbs (2,079 kg). Quite the hefty bugger for a camper that is just shy of 18 feet (5.5 m) and stands at a bit over 10.5 ft (3.2 m) tall.
One reason for the weight has a whole lot to do with the running gear underneath this camper, a setup that is independent one with a shear spring setup of around 5 inches of travel and even tested in Moab; it’s completed by MoRyde. According to sources, the reason for shear springs as opposed to airbags or traditional springs has to do with keeping the weight down as much as possible.
Photo: Forest River Inc This wheel action also means that we can easily break away from the tarmac and gravel roads and really venture deep into the wild, but it also means less stress on your camper’s shell, helping prolong its life, and some current camper owners do purchase and used preloved Pause Reboot trailers and are more than happy with the state they’re in.
Aside from the suspension, people also rave about the wood-free construction, standing up to the elements year after year. Just keep in mind that maintenance and upkeep is a must, even for a camper of this sort of construction.
As for the living experience we can tap into once we’ve reached our hidden haven, owners really enjoy the features that Forest River includes in the unit, mentioning that "it has everything we could need and ask for, and nothing extra we don’t use.”
Photo: Forest River Inc Features like the outdoor kitchen and cooler are among the loved ones, and so is the side-mounted table located near the rear, but inside, is really where Forest River shows off that they too can craft a camper worth the bucks; typically, this brand has a bad wrap when it comes to campers, but the Pause Reboot lineup does seem to “reboot” our confidence in the brand. It’s as if Forest River either makes campers people hate or love.
The interior of the 14.3 surprised me in the fact that it includes yet another complete kitchen, this time with standing fridge, a dining area that can be transformed into an extra bed for a child, a matrimonial bed for two, and even a dry bath. Yes, the toilet sits separate the shower but there is no vanity.
This is a trait that we rarely see in a camper of this size, but as I mentioned, Forest River really went all out on this lineup.
Photo: Forest River Inc Storage is clearly not a problem for the 14.3 either, with the interior displaying ample options for your gear and personal belongings, but outside we also find a neat little platform at the rear of the camper that allows us to put down a couple of e-bikes, climbing and fishing gear, and whatever else you can secure to the space; it can handle 300 lbs. A spare tire is also usually found mounted to this tray. The GVWR of the 14.3 stands at 5,868 lbs (2,662 kgs).
While there is a large nose-cone box mounted in the 14.3’s frame, it’s onto more important traits of this unit, like the off-grid features and systems that are in place as standard. None other than Victron is called upon to handle our power needs and instead of boring you with a long list of systems, inverters, and batteries, I invite you to check out the clip on a 2026 14.3 below to see what’s in store.
Photo: Forest River Inc Keep in mind that off-grid capabilities are expandable, and we can tap into 800 W of solar and 1,296 Ah of lithium. When’s the last time you heard of a Forest River with this much kick?
Frankly, it’s these reasons and a few others that force the Pause Reboot 14.3 to carry such a high price tag, and while Forest River isn’t always the first choice for Americans, in the past year or so, I have been seeing some changes in the brand, with units that seem to be designed and built with a bit more attention than, let’s say, five years ago.
Would you rock a Pause Reboot 14.3? Drop your comments below.

Posted By: Cecilia Jamasmie November 19, 2026
Ivanhoe Electric (NYSE American: IE; TSX: IE), backed by mining billionaire Robert Friedland, has discovered high-grade copper-gold-silver mineralization at its Gleeson project in southeastern Arizona, making it the company’s top exploration priority.
The company reporte d Thursday that drilling identified two mineralized zones, including 123.6 metres grading 0.91% copper, 0.44 gram of gold per tonne and 5.27 grams of silver per tonne from a depth of 601.7 metres. The interval included 71.03 metres grading 1.38% copper, 0.52 gram of gold and 6.73 grams of silver.
“These initial drill results are some of the best copper-gold-silver intercepts drilled in the Western United States in the last 10 years,” Executive Chairman Friedland and President and CEO Taylor Melvin said in a joint statement.
The discovery, 45 km north of Arizona’s historic Bisbee mining district, could provide another growth opportunity alongside Ivanhoe Electric’s Santa Cruz copper project near Casa Grande, where it plans to produce refined copper domestically.
Copper drop
Shares in Ivanhoe Electric fell 2.6% to C$8.33 apiece by Thursday afternoon, valuing the company at about C$1.33 billion. Wider markets declined as investors appeared to be selling on the rally created by the widely anticipated Anthropic initial public offering.
The drill results come as copper prices plunged about 6% this week to $12,471 per tonne on the London Metal Exchange, their lowest since April. Investors have been unwinding bets on artificial intelligence-driven demand and potential US tariffs on refined copper, with the sell-off accelerating after billionaire investor Stan Druckenmiller turned bearish .
The decline contrasts with tight physical supplies in China, where the Yangshan copper import premium reached a record $360 per tonne, up from less than $100 in September. Shanghai Futures Exchange inventories fell 18% over the week to 27,600 tonnes, their lowest since December 2023, highlighting the divide between investor sentiment and physical market conditions.
Two zones
Ivanhoe Electric spent $4.7 million (C$6.7 million) on exploration and evaluation at Gleeson in the quarter to Sept. 30, up from $219,000 a year earlier, the company said in a filing. Two rigs are working towards 16,000 metres by year-end, including drilling completed since November 2025.
Drilling at Gleeson has outlined an upper copper-gold-silver-bearing breccia zone spanning approximately 500 by 500 metres, beginning around 600 metres below surface. The mineralization thickens southwestward and remains open in several directions.
A second hole, CGD26-TR-008, returned 381.66 metres grading 0.34% copper, 0.29 gram of gold and 1.07 grams of silver per tonne from 587.85 metres. It included 16.2 metres grading 1.04% copper and a separate 41.51-metre interval grading 1.23 grams of gold.
Deeper drilling, below 1,000 metres, identified intrusive-hosted, skarn and carbonate-replacement mineralization containing copper, gold, silver and zinc. The system extends roughly 800 metres north to south and 600 metres east to west, with further potential to the west.
“The initial drill holes at Gleeson are the most impressive I have seen in my 20-year career at an early-stage exploration project,” Senior Vice-President of Exploration Alex Neufeld said.
Bisbee district
Neufeld compared Gleeson’s geology with the nearby Bisbee district, which produced more than 200 million tonnes of ore over 133 years.
Ivanhoe Electric controls approximately 20,000 acres of mineral rights and more than 2,000 acres of private surface rights at Gleeson, although drilling has tested only a small portion of the property.
Since November 2025, the company has completed 11 drill holes, receiving full assays for seven and partial results for two. Two rigs are operating, with 16,000 metres of drilling targeted by year-end. Additional holes have encountered visible sulphide mineralization, including deeper carbonate-replacement zones beginning around 1,250 metres below surface.
Gleeson remains an early-stage discovery without a defined mineral resource or demonstrated economic viability. Further drilling must establish the continuity, scale and true widths of the mineralized zones.
American copper
The discovery strengthens Ivanhoe Electric’s Arizona portfolio as it advances Santa Cruz, a proposed high-grade underground mine on private land near Casa Grande.
Santa Cruz is designed to produce refined copper cathode through hydrometallurgical processing, including solvent extraction and electrowinning, eliminating the need for conventional smelting or overseas concentrate refining.
The approach could help supply US manufacturers directly while reducing exposure to international processing bottlenecks and certain trade risks, aligning with Washington’s efforts to secure domestic copper supplies for electricity networks, defence and manufacturing.
Friedland, whose ventures have included some of the world’s largest copper discoveries, sees Gleeson as a potential new mineral district in the American Southwest.

Torex Resources (TSX: TXR; NYSE: TXR) has won Toronto Stock Exchange approval to renew a share buyback covering about 10% of its public float, two days after the Mexico-focused miner began trading in New York.
The renewed bid allows Torex to repurchase up to 7.18 million common shares from Nov. 23 through Nov. 22, 2027. Under the previous authorization, which expires Nov. 20, Torex bought back 6.26 million of a permitted 8.13 million shares through Nov. 11.

The buyback is part of Torex’s plan to return $350 million to shareholders in 2026 through repurchases and dividends. It had returned $270.8 million by Sept. 30, or about 77% of that target, the company said in its third-quarter results .
The company plans to fund any repurchases from available working capital. It can buy shares through the Toronto or New York exchanges or alternative trading systems in Canada and the United States. It will cancel any shares it buys.
TSX purchases are generally capped at 129,854 shares a day, with one block purchase above that limit allowed per calendar week. Torex can suspend repurchases at any time and says its decisions will depend on market conditions, its share price and other opportunities to invest.

EICMA 2026 • 2026 EICMA's Speed Legends Exhibit Was Not To Be Missed – See the Bikes That Paved MotoGP History
Car Nut Bought Split-Bumper 1972 Camaro Sight Unseen, Who Can Tell if It's a Real RS, or a Tribute
46 photos
Photo: YouTube/Show Me Your Car
Chevrolet executives nearly slipped on a giant banana peel in 1972 and axed the Camaro moniker altogether, turning Detroit into a slapstick comedy of corporate panic. A grueling 174-day strike at Norwood jammed the assembly line like a cream pie in the face, while incoming 1973 bumper rules forced the scrapping of 1,100 unfinished cars. Brass panicked over low output before cooler heads saved the badge from becoming a punchline.
The Camaro went on the rollercoaster of its life in the seventies, from the abyss of the early years to the peak of 1979, the greatest moment of the moniker (in sales, anyway). One of those ‘72s recently caught the eye of Craig Glenn, the roaming YouTuber from the Show Me Your Car channel. The car belongs to Mike Darty, who bought it back in May sight unseen as a birthday present to himself from Streetside Classics in Atlanta, Georgia, and just got it back on the road.
According to the Streetside Classics listing , the car is a 1972 Chevrolet Camaro RS tribute, and the asking price was $30,995 with 68,060 miles shown, and a 350 V8 paired with a 3-speed automatic transmission. The listing highlighted Mohave Gold paint, a crisp white vinyl top, Covert interior trim, 15-inch rally wheels with 235/60R15 tires, a 10-bolt rear axle, and a numbers-matching 350 engine.
Under the hood, the spec sheet notes a numbers-matching 350 cubic-inch V8 painted Chevy Orange with a FiTech fuel injection system, controller in the glove box, Edelbrock Performer EPS intake, polished Chevrolet valve covers, and long tube headers feeding dual exhaust with Borla mufflers. Power steering, air conditioning, front power disc and rear power drum brakes, and a RetroSound radio round out the build.
Photo: YouTube/Show Me Your Car Mike adds his own garage-floor slapstick to the story, having fitted fresh front suspension components, new brakes, and black wheels with fresh tires after the dry-rotted rubber nearly gave up the ghost. He also washed the car after towing it back from Lebanon so the white vinyl top would dry on the drive home, keeping a clean cabin with working lights, covert custom cloth, and a 130-mph speedometer.
Across its full run, the Camaro moniker spans production years 1966 to 2002 and 2009 to 2023 across six generations, with model years running from 1967 through 2002 and 2010 through 2024. The second generation from 1970 through 1981 holds the longest production run at 12 model years, surviving fuel scares, shifting regulations, and plenty of Detroit boardroom pratfalls.
In total volume, the second generation leads the entire Camaro family with 1,959,879 units built over its 12 model years, outpacing every other era by sheer cumulative weight. By contrast, the first generation from 1967 through 1969 takes the highest yearly average at roughly 233,046 cars per model year across 699,138 total builds, proving how quickly the pony car caught fire out of the gate.
Photo: YouTube/Show Me Your Car For the sake of historic accuracy, we should point out that the 1969 production year was extended through November 1969, instead of ending in July as traditionally. The cause of delay was tooling issues, forcing the execs to prolong the first generation by a few extra months. That’s the reason for a 243k- pony car production record scored that season.
For 1972, total Camaro production landed at 68,651 cars in standard reference tallies, as labor disputes tripped up Chevrolet at every turn. Out the 365 days between one production year to the next, the 1972 season was marred by 174 strike days. Buyers fortunate enough to get one could order the base Sport Coupe, the Z22 Rally Sport package, the Z27 Super Sport package, or the Z28 Special Performance Package. Convertibles were off the books in the second generation, leaving coupes to carry the show.
Powertrains for 1972 debuted SAE net horsepower ratings, starting with the 250-cubic-inch inline-six rated at 110 horsepower and the 307 V8 rated at 130 horsepower. Small-block 350 V8 choices included the two-barrel L65 at 165 horsepower and four-barrel L48 at 200 horsepower, while the Z28-exclusive solid-lifter LT-1 350 made 255 horsepower and the big-block 396/402 LS3 delivered 240 horsepower.
Photo: YouTube/Show Me Your Car What set the 1972 RS apart from regular Camaros was its split front bumperette arrangement and body-colored grille surround with round auxiliary and parking lights tucked beside the headlights. Non-RS models used a full front bumper and lower square parking lights instead. Meanwhile, Z28 and SS focused on powertrain hardware, whereas RS was a trim package available on base, SS, or Z28 cars.
Compared with first-generation RS models, the second-generation RS dropped hideaway headlights completely—a slapstick relief for anyone tired of vacuum doors sticking like stubborn dresser drawers. It also traded full front bumpers for split bumperettes and replaced dual headlights per side with single round lamps rather than a quad headlight layout, giving the early second-gen RS its unmistakable gaping fish mouth face.
Production numbers for 1972 break down into 4,821 six-cylinder Sport Coupes and 63,830 V8 Sport Coupes, spread between 11,364 Rally Sports, 6,562 SSs, and 2,575 Z28s. 27,009 cars received the L65 350 two-barrel V8 and 970 Super Sports received the LS3 396/402 big-block V8.
Photo: YouTube/Show Me Your Car Transmission choices for 1972 include 4,127 M20 wide-ratio 4-speeds, 942 M21 close-ratio 4-speeds, and 767 M22 heavy-duty close-ratio 4-speeds, plus 4,462 Powerglide 2-speed automatics and 7,302 Turbo Hydra-Matic 3-speed automatics alongside standard 3-speed manuals.
Base price for the cheapest 1972 Camaro—the six-cylinder Sport Coupe—was $2,729.70, while the V8 coupe started at $2,819.70. The RS package cost $118. Rounding out the 1972 order sheet, RPO Z27 (Super Sport) cost $306.35, while the Z28 was $769.15.

Five U.S. regional grid operators have submitted sweeping tariff reforms to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) that could fundamentally change how data centers and other large electricity consumers connect to the transmission system, secure access to generating capacity, and pay for the necessary infrastructure.
The proposals, filed Nov. 13 and 16 in response to FERC’s June 18 show-cause orders , mark a broad effort, seeking to accelerate large-load energization without compromising grid reliability or shifting the costs of new infrastructure to existing customers. Broadly, the grid operators appear to be willing to adopt a 50-MW threshold to identify large loads, but their proposals are substantially different in the conditions under which those customers could obtain transmission service, the capacity they would need to secure, and the operational and financial obligations they would assume.
Among the most significant developments is the expansion of transmission service options that could allow large loads to withdraw electricity from the grid on a non-firm basis, potentially before all the network upgrades required for firm service are completed.
Three grid operators—the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) , under its proposed Grid Responsive Integration Transmission Service (GRITS); the New York Independent System Operator (NYISO) , as part of its new Large Load Integration Procedures (LLIP) and associated market rules; and ISO New England (ISO-NE) —have proposed mechanisms that would use wholesale electricity prices to trigger reductions in grid withdrawals, though the thresholds, market mechanics, and associated capacity obligations differ.
The filings also advance markedly different approaches to resource adequacy. Under its proposed “ Bring Your Own New Capacity ” (BYONC) requirement, ISO-NE would require large loads seeking firm transmission service to secure incremental new capacity. NYISO would allow large loads whose addition would adversely affect resource adequacy to secure firm withdrawal rights through long-term arrangements with qualifying resources that need not be physically co-located. The California Independent System Operator (CAISO) , by contrast, argues that a customer-specific generation procurement requirement is unnecessary under its existing resource adequacy framework and has proposed a Flexible Interim Load Interconnection (FILI) arrangement to accommodate earlier energization subject to transmission constraints.
PJM Interconnection , meanwhile, has proposed a Fast Energization Process that would consolidate generation interconnection and large-load transmission service studies into a single 12-month cycle. In a separate filing, PJM also proposed ride-through requirements , which will establish “thresholds through which data centers must remain connected to the grid, rather than switching to backup generation, to avoid large transfers of load that can destabilize the system.” PJM’s transmission owners, acting collectively under the Consolidated Transmission Owners Agreement, have separately proposed a new methodology that would distribute responsibility for the costs of transmission reinforcements identified through that process among transmission customers and generation developers.
A Region-Specific Regulatory Approach
The November filings stem from six proceedings FERC initiated June 18 under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act (FPA), after the Commission preliminarily found that existing regional transmission tariffs may be unjust and unreasonable or unduly discriminatory or preferential in their treatment of large loads. The orders identified five broad areas for reform: efficient transmission service studies, rules for co-located loads and loads served by behind-the-meter generation, transmission services for flexible loads, studies of generating facilities serving electrically proximate large loads and co-located loads, and transparency in infrastructure costs and cost allocation. As significantly, FERC directed the grid operators to separately address how they intend to ensure adequate generation capacity to serve existing and new large loads.
The Commission provided an avenue for each regional transmission organization (RTO) and independent system operator (ISO) to propose tariff revisions tailored to its existing transmission, market, and regulatory framework under Section 205 of the FPA. On Aug. 14, the Commission granted requests to hold the show-cause proceedings in abeyance to accommodate those filings, establishing response deadlines of Nov. 16 for five grid operators and Nov. 20 for Southwest Power Pool (SPP) . ISO-NE submitted its proposal Nov. 13, followed on Nov. 16 by CAISO, MISO, NYISO, PJM, and PJM’s transmission owners. SPP’s filing is expected Friday.
PJM’s filings also address outstanding compliance obligations from a separate proceeding FERC initiated in February 2025 on the co-location of large loads at generating facilities. The Commission first advanced new transmission service options for co-located loads in PJM before proposing their broader application across all six jurisdictional regional grid operators.
The June orders also advance objectives outlined in an Oct. 23, 2025, directive from Energy Secretary Chris Wright , who invoked Section 403 of the Department of Energy (DOE) Organization Act to initiate rulemaking procedures on large-load interconnection to the interstate transmission system. FERC opted to pursue region-specific reforms under Section 206 of the FPA while keeping the broader rulemaking proceeding (Docket No. RM26-4-000) open, including to address large-load integration outside organized regional markets.
“The tailored show cause orders encourage each RTO/ISO to work with its transmission owners and stakeholders to address the challenges to timely interconnect large loads. This region-specific approach has the advantage of allowing each RTO/ISO to develop its unique solutions. For example, in contrast to a rulemaking that would propose uniform national standards, the show cause orders allow FERC to recognize different paths to progress in this area, such as the tariff progress already made by the PJM Interconnection, LLC (PJM) and SPP regions,” FERC’s Office of Public Participation explained in guidance updated Oct. 19 .
The November proposals, notably, remain subject to FERC review, and several of the most significant reforms would require additional tariff filings, stakeholder proceedings, or market software development before implementation.
Transmission Access and Resource Adequacy
At the heart of the November reforms is a distinction between two types of flexibility: the ability of a large load to operate temporarily under transmission constraints while network upgrades are completed, and its willingness to accept restrictions on electricity withdrawals as a long-term condition of service. But another major consideration is resource adequacy. Even where sufficient transmission capability exists to serve a new industrial facility or data center, a region may lack sufficient generating resources to reliably accommodate that demand. The proposed tariffs address both constraints through different combinations of transmission service rights, mandatory curtailment, and capacity procurement obligations.
MISO. Under its proposed Interim Network Integration Transmission Service (NITS) and optional Firm Service Step Up process , a large load could initially receive a combination of firm and non-firm transmission service and progressively convert portions of its interim service to firm service as additional transmission capability becomes available. The load would remain subject to existing capacity procurement requirements throughout the transition.
GRITS [ Grid Responsive Integration Transmission Service ], by contrast, would establish an ongoing alternative to conventional network transmission service. MISO illustrates the arrangement using a 500-MW facility that elects to secure 200 MW of firm transmission service and up to 300 MW of non-firm service. While both quantities would be governed by a single service agreement, MISO would model them at separate commercial pricing nodes to account for differences in reservation rights, interruption requirements, billing, and capacity obligations. Firm GRITS could be reserved for periods of at least one year, while non-firm GRITS could be reserved for periods ranging from one day to one month.
Under its proposed GRITS market rules , MISO would require market participants representing non-firm demand to submit price-sensitive demand bids and would incorporate that demand into its security-constrained unit commitment and economic dispatch processes. Non-firm demand would be subject to interruption when the locational marginal price (LMP) at its commercial pricing node exceeds $100/MWh.
The proposed GRITS Offer Cap corresponds to the first non-zero step of MISO’s market-wide short-term reserve demand curve, which establishes a price for increasingly scarce short-term operating reserves. MISO intends the threshold to restrict non-firm consumption before an operating reserve shortfall occurs. Historical market data suggest that the threshold would permit service in more than 95% of hours, MISO said. However, a capacity advisory in the applicable local balancing authority area would require curtailment of the entire non-firm GRITS load even if the LMP remains below $100/MWh.
The firm portion of a GRITS customer’s demand would remain in MISO’s coincident peak demand forecast and retain the corresponding obligation to procure Zonal Resource Credits (ZRCs), which represent accredited capacity under MISO’s resource adequacy framework. Non-firm GRITS demand may be excluded from the obligation to procure ZRCs, in which case it would not be included in the forecast. Unlike Interim NITS, whose customers retain capacity obligations as they progress toward firm transmission service, GRITS would allow customers to permanently limit the quantity of capacity they must procure by accepting corresponding restrictions on electricity withdrawals.
MISO would also prohibit non-firm GRITS demand from participating as a Demand Response Resource, Load Modifying Resource, or Emergency Demand Response resource. MISO said the Demand Response Resource prohibition is consistent with FERC Order No. 745, which governs compensation for demand response in organized wholesale energy markets, and that the Load Modifying Resource prohibition follows from non-firm GRITS demand not having an obligation to procure ZRCs.
ISO New England. ISO-NE proposes three new transmission service categories: Firm Contract Demand Service, Non-Firm Contract Demand Service, and Interim Contract Demand Service. Under its proposed Bring Your Own New Capacity (BYONC) framework, outlined in Section II.59 of its Open Access Transmission Tariff (OATT) , large-load customers seeking firm service would be required to designate, or arrange for the designation of, sufficient new capacity resources to meet their requested firm demand. Customers would receive interim service for that demand until the designated resources achieve commercial operation.
Essentially, the proposed provisions would put developers on notice of the new capacity requirements ahead of a more detailed tariff filing anticipated in 2027. Significant questions remain unresolved, including how to define “new” capacity, accredit resources, set locational requirements, and treat designated resources under ISO-NE’s Pay-for-Performance settlement mechanism. Large loads receiving interim or non-firm contract demand service would be excluded from the region’s Installed Capacity Requirement and exempt from capacity charges.
ISO-NE would, however, exempt qualifying demand at facilities already in operation or sufficiently under construction as of June 18, 2026. If a facility’s gross peak demand increases by 50 MW or more above its exempt demand, the incremental demand would become subject to the new large-load requirements. The previously exempt demand would transition to Firm Contract Demand Service and become subject to the operational requirements but would remain exempt from the new study and capacity designation requirements.
ISO-NE has proposed a Large Load Re-Dispatch Price of $250/MWh for both interim and non-firm service, which corresponds to the penalty factor for replacement reserves, a voluntary reliability service in New England. Based on hourly load-zone prices from 2021 through 2025, ISO-NE said the proposed price occurred in approximately 1% of hours.
But, unlike MISO’s proposed requirement for price-sensitive demand bids, ISO-NE would make the submission of demand bids optional. In the absence of a bid, the grid operator would schedule consumption based on the load’s submitted demand forecast, its authorized transmission service quantities, and the redispatch price. The proposal would also allow qualifying co-located or electrically proximate generation to satisfy part or all of a redispatch instruction, potentially reducing the need to curtail the facility’s electricity consumption. ISO-NE plans to review the $250/MWh threshold through its stakeholder process beginning in 2027.
NYISO. Under its proposed Large Load Integration Procedures , NYISO would determine eligibility for Firm Withdrawal Service through a project-specific resource adequacy assessment over a 10-year study horizon.
For projects subject to the standard assessment, a large load that degrades resource adequacy by the equivalent of 25 MW or less would be eligible for its full requested amount of firm service, subject to resolution of transmission security violations. NYISO says the 25-MW tolerance accounts for inherent limitations in the precision of probabilistic resource adequacy models. If the degradation exceeds 25 MW, NYISO would determine how much of the requested service must be non-firm to restore the system’s loss-of-load expectation to its pre-project level.
Developers could mitigate adverse resource adequacy impacts through two mechanisms: a Co-Located Arrangement, under which the associated resource and large load share a point of interconnection, or a Partner Resource Arrangement, under which the associated resource could be located elsewhere within the same capacity region. Both arrangements would have a 15-year term.
During that period, the portion of a large load’s firm withdrawal rights attributable to the associated resource would remain contingent on the resource’s continued participation in NYISO’s Installed Capacity (ICAP) market. If the resource enters an ICAP-ineligible forced outage, is mothballed or retired, or otherwise exits the capacity market, the corresponding portion of the load’s service would be reclassified as Non-Firm Withdrawal Service. Firm rights could be restored if the resource resumes eligible participation. After the 15-year term expires, those withdrawal rights would no longer depend on the associated resource’s continued capacity market participation.
NYISO also proposes a category of State Exempt Large Load Projects. The New York State Department of Public Service could identify projects for exemption through a mechanism established in the New York State Public Service Commission’s ongoing large-load interconnection proceeding. NYISO would assess the collective resource adequacy impact of those projects under an alternative standard. If their combined impact does not violate applicable New York State Reliability Council resource adequacy criteria over the first five years of the study, the projects would be eligible for their full requested amounts of firm service, subject to transmission security requirements.
NYISO’s proposed $200/MWh maximum bid price for Non-Firm Withdrawal Service draws on a different reliability mechanism from those proposed by MISO and ISO-NE: transmission scarcity pricing. Under NYISO’s existing Constraint Specific Shortage Pricing mechanism, a six-step transmission demand curve produces a constraint price of $4,000/MWh at full utilization of a transmission facility’s Constraint Reliability Margin.
To establish its bid cap, NYISO applied a 5% materiality threshold derived from the North American Electric Reliability Corp.’s (NERC’s) Transmission Loading Relief procedures. A non-firm load whose shift factor, a measure of how strongly its withdrawals affect flows across a constraint, meets that 5% threshold would, except in rare cases, receive a nodal price of $200/MWh when the constraint price reaches $4,000/MWh. The proposed bid cap is intended to allow market dispatch to curtail non-firm loads before manual operator intervention becomes necessary.
NYISO would exclude large loads taking any amount of Non-Firm Withdrawal Service from its Demand Side Resource programs, even if a portion of their demand receives firm service. The grid operator has also proposed a separate System Reliability Benefit Fee to allocate capacity market costs to demand without firm withdrawal rights in an amount roughly commensurate with the benefits that demand receives from ICAP resources.
PJM. PJM’s proposed Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, and Interim NITS would establish a framework for accommodating flexible demand without a uniform wholesale price-based curtailment threshold.
Under its proposed Part XI tariff provisions , PJM would assign firm contract demand service the same curtailment priority as conventional NITS and firm point-to-point transmission service. Non-firm contract demand service and Interim NITS would have the same curtailment priority as non-firm point-to-point service.
Firm contract demand service would provide both energy and capacity, and customers taking it would retain applicable generation capacity obligations. Non-firm contract demand service would provide energy on an as-available basis. PJM describes Interim NITS as an energy-only service that is not capacity backed, and PJM’s transmission owners said customers taking it would not be assessed generation capacity charges, unlike MISO’s proposed treatment of Interim NITS. The transmission owners have proposed separate rate methodologies for the new transmission services.
To prevent customers from switching between firm and non-firm contract demand service to avoid capacity costs, PJM would prohibit customers from obtaining non-firm contract demand service for any portion of a load previously served under firm contract demand service for five years following the effective date of the relevant transmission service agreement.
CAISO. California, meanwhile, has proposed a substantially different approach that seeks to preserve its existing transmission access and resource adequacy frameworks. Under Flexible Interim Load Interconnection (FILI), participating transmission owners would develop project-specific operating restrictions to allow large loads to energize before completion of required transmission upgrades.
The restrictions could include preset operating schedules, enforceable operating requirements, automated remedial action schemes, or load curtailment performed by the transmission owner after a transmission contingency occurs. CAISO has declined to propose a uniform duration or capacity limit for FILI arrangements. The grid operator plans to begin a separate stakeholder initiative in 2027 to explore permanent flexible load interconnection, which could allow customers to avoid certain transmission network upgrades by accepting ongoing restrictions on electricity withdrawals.
Because CAISO does not administer a centralized forward capacity market, responsibility for procuring adequate resources rests principally on load-serving entities (LSEs) under requirements established by the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) and other applicable local regulatory authorities.
“This distinction can remove an important barrier to timely service: a large load customer need not independently secure new generating capacity or satisfy a separate CAISO forward-capacity-market requirement as a condition of interconnection,” CAISO explained in its Nov. 16 filing . “The CAISO has no centralized forward capacity market; instead, serving load remains subject to the resource adequacy obligations applicable to its load-serving entity (LSE) and the requirements of the relevant local regulatory authority. The absence of a customer-specific generation requirement therefore does not eliminate advance capacity procurement obligations or guarantee immediate service at every location.”
CAISO acknowledged that the effectiveness of its framework depends on timely resource procurement and development and that large loads could materialize faster than existing forecasts and procurement processes anticipate. The grid operator said it intends to continue evaluating those risks in coordination with California’s energy agencies.
