Reengineering Interconnection Studies
As the filings indicate, echoing industry concerns, the rapid emergence of large electricity consumers has exposed limitations in traditional transmission study processes, which generally evaluate new generating facilities and requests to serve new demand through separate procedures. Independent studies of a proposed 500-MW power plant and a corresponding 500-MW load, for example, could identify transmission reinforcements that a coordinated assessment of generation injections and load withdrawals might reduce or eliminate.
PJM. Among the most extensive reforms proposed in November is PJM’s Fast Energization Process , which would consolidate studies for generation and merchant transmission interconnection, long-term firm transmission service, and large-load transmission service into a single 12-month cycle—approximately half the duration of its existing interconnection cycle. The proposal advances objectives outlined in PJM’s five-year strategy, published in August .
Under proposed revisions to Part VIII of its tariff, PJM would replace three system impact study phases with an approximately four-month screening phase and a single system impact study. Two rounds of screening would provide preliminary estimates of required transmission reinforcements, their costs, and construction durations. Developers would have an opportunity after each round to assess the results and determine whether to proceed. Negotiations over final agreements would begin concurrently with the system impact study.
Perhaps more significantly, PJM would move away from identifying individual transmission upgrades attributable to specific interconnection requests and instead develop a portfolio of Interconnection Reliability Reinforcements (IRRs) to accommodate the generation and transmission service requests in each cycle.
“The Fast Energization Process moves PJM away from identifying specific upgrades and tying them to specific projects. PJM instead will analyze upgrades and reinforcements as enabling the entire Cycle cohort of generation projects and transmission service requests,” PJM explained in its FERC filing. “The resulting IRRs are optimized for the whole Cycle, which eliminates overlapping or duplicative upgrades for generation and load. This approach also allows a fractional amount of generating capacity to become deliverable faster and with greater certainty, rather than only upon completion of all required Network Upgrades.”
The accelerated process would, however, impose more stringent project readiness requirements. Generation developers would have to submit readiness deposits in full at application, and transmission customers seeking service on behalf of large loads would have to execute cost recovery agreements with the relevant transmission owners before entering the process. Physical project modifications after application would require developers to withdraw and resubmit their projects in a subsequent cycle.
PJM also proposes a 14-week Early Application Engagement period to test developers’ models and provide feedback and guidance on project readiness. The grid operator anticipates substantial time savings from automation, an approach it has already begun deploying.
As POWER reported in April 2025 , PJM launched a multiyear collaboration with Google and Tapestry, Alphabet’s grid technology moonshot, to accelerate its interconnection process through artificial intelligence (AI). In a Nov. 10 report on the deployment of its HyperQ platform , Tapestry reported a 60-fold acceleration in the intake and initial review of site control documentation. The tool compressed a two-month manual process to less than 24 hours and produced readiness reports for 811 generation interconnection applications representing 220 GW of potential capacity at a median computational runtime of six minutes and 15 seconds per application. PJM, however, has stressed that its subject matter experts remain “in absolute control,” and Tapestry said PJM’s engineers perform the final compliance determinations.
The reported performance gains apply specifically to application intake and site control verification, not to engineering studies. Tapestry’s subsequent work includes technical data validation for interconnection model files, single-line diagrams, and network configuration data. PJM is in tandem developing additional modeling and analytical tools to accelerate power flow and dynamic studies.
MISO. Under its proposed Large Load Project Review (LLPR), outlined in revisions to Attachment FF of its tariff , MISO would complete three study cycles in each 365-day period. Each successive cycle would incorporate transmission system changes identified in the previous completed cycle to reduce restudy risk.
The proposal would also incorporate MISO’s previously filed Large Load Addition Resource Study (LARS), submitted Oct. 2 in Docket No. ER27-25. Unlike PJM’s proposed consolidation of generation and load requests across an entire study cycle, MISO’s LARS specifically addresses projects involving large loads of at least 200 MW that have formally partnered with a generator for a minimum of 15 years.
LLPR applications would require substantial preliminary engineering work, including a transmission owner’s interconnection study report, electrical models, single-line diagrams, identified upgrades, estimated costs, and proposed cost allocation. Applicants would also have to submit a nonrefundable $250,000 application fee and a $100,000 study deposit.
ISO New England. ISO-NE proposes to accept large-load transmission service applications on a rolling basis and assign completed applications positions in a dedicated large-load queue. The grid operator and the interconnecting transmission owner would use reasonable efforts to complete a system impact study within 90 days of execution of the applicable study agreement. Interconnection studies for qualifying co-located and electrically proximate generating facilities could proceed concurrently.
NYISO. Under its proposed Large Load Integration Procedures, NYISO would accept applications on a rolling basis and study projects in successive groups. Each of up to two initial study rounds would include a resource adequacy and modeling period and a 90-day system impact study. NYISO and the applicable transmission owners would subsequently undertake a more comprehensive Assessment of Load Integration and facilities studies in parallel.
NYISO estimates the overall process would take approximately 18 months to two years, depending on when a project enters the study cycle. NYISO acknowledged that the process would take longer than the 60- to 90-day duration contemplated in FERC’s show-cause order but argued the timeframe is reasonable given the scope of its study process. To accommodate additional applicants, NYISO would overlap initial studies for a new cycle with the more advanced assessments of the preceding cycle.
CAISO. California would preserve the existing division of responsibilities between CAISO and its participating transmission owners, which conduct load interconnection studies under their respective tariffs. CAISO proposes to coordinate and review those studies on a monthly basis to accommodate the transmission owners’ study timelines. The grid operator has prioritized reforms applicable to stand-alone loads and co-located generation and plans to examine separate provisions for electrically proximate generation and load through a future stakeholder initiative.
Alternative Transmission Technologies. FERC’s June orders also identified the need to evaluate alternative transmission technologies that could reduce the cost or shorten the construction schedules of required infrastructure. MISO, for example, would require transmission owners to document their consideration of alternative transmission technologies and grid-enhancing technologies in interconnection study reports submitted through the LLPR process.
Engineering for Co-Located and Flexible Loads
Beyond the changes to transmission planning and interconnection procedures, the November filings address a series of operational challenges associated with large loads. Recent disturbances in PJM have underscored the urgency of establishing more stringent technical requirements.
On July 22, 2026, nearly 3.9 GW of data center demand in PJM unexpectedly transferred from utility power to onsite generation in response to a transmission disturbance. System frequency reached 60.092 Hz, and voltage peaked at approximately 1.138 per unit, or 13.8% above its nominal reference value. The disturbance followed a 1.5-GW load transfer on July 10, 2024, and a 1.8-GW event on Feb. 17, 2025.
“These events affected system voltages, frequency, power flows and generator behavior in the Dominion transmission zone and across the entire Eastern Interconnection. And while safely managed by PJM’s Control Center, the scale and speed of the unexpected load transfers posed serious threats to the reliability and safety of the grid,” PJM said in a Nov. 16 Inside Lines post on its proposed operational requirements for large computational loads .
Voltage and Frequency Ride-Through. PJM, which already serves approximately 10 GW of large computational loads and forecasts 30 GW of data center-driven peak load growth between 2024 and 2030, has separately filed tariff revisions in Docket No. ER27-522-000 that would establish a category of Large Computational Load. The definition would encompass large loads of 50 MW or more that have at least 25 MW of maximum demand served through power electronic conversion equipment.
The proposed tariff revisions would require PJM to establish minimum voltage and frequency ride-through requirements in its manuals. PJM has requested a Jan. 16, 2027, effective date. Transitional facilities—those for which customers have formally initiated interconnection studies, executed qualifying interconnection or service agreements, begun construction, or reached commercial operation before the effective date—would have until Jan. 16, 2028, or one year after their commercial operation date, whichever is later, to comply.
The filing also establishes a framework for additional operational requirements, including ramp rates, electromagnetic transient performance, protective equipment, metering, telemetry, and communications. The regional provisions would complement ongoing efforts by the North American Electric Reliability Corp. (NERC) to develop mandatory reliability standards for computational loads.
Enforcing Withdrawal Limits. Co-located generation presents a separate operational challenge. A 500-MW data center that receives 450 MW from onsite generation and withdraws 50 MW from the transmission system could suddenly require its entire 500 MW from the grid if the generating plant trips. Unless the transmission system can accommodate the additional withdrawals, the facility must have alternative supply or controls capable of reducing demand.
Under PJM’s proposed Part XI provisions, eligible customers would be responsible for the hardware and software necessary to enforce authorized withdrawals, including, where required, fully redundant special protection schemes. An initial misoperation of a required control or protection scheme would result in suspension of withdrawals under the applicable transmission service agreement for up to 120 days, subject to mutual agreement to adjust that period. A second misoperation would result in termination of the agreement.
MISO similarly would authorize transmission owners to remotely disconnect customers taking non-firm GRITS that fail to interrupt demand as directed. Repeated violations could result in additional financial penalties and possible termination of service. ISO-NE would require demand forecasts, telemetry, communications, and equipment to facilitate remote disconnection. CAISO’s proposed FILI arrangements, meanwhile, would establish project-specific curtailment requirements, response times, and conditions for restoration of service.
Who Pays for Grid Expansion?
Perhaps the most significant commercial changes accompany PJM’s proposed consolidation of generation and load studies. The PJM transmission owners, notably, have proposed revisions to Schedule 12 of the regional tariff that would establish a distinct methodology for allocating the costs of Interconnection Reliability Reinforcements identified through each study cycle.
For the first 15 years, costs would be allocated to transmission zones containing large-load transmission service requests evaluated during the applicable cycle. The methodology would account for the location of the reinforcements and the modeled electrical impacts of large loads on transmission constraints. After 15 years, the remaining costs would be allocated under the prevailing Schedule 12 methodology for regional reliability projects.
Generation developers would also contribute through a proposed Generator Reliability Reinforcement Fee. PJM would convert each generator’s allocated share of the estimated portfolio capital cost into a levelized annual payment over 15 years, based on a capital recovery factor derived from the transmission owners’ weighted average costs of capital. Proceeds would be credited to customers in zones allocated reinforcement costs.
“In PJM, load pays for transmission service. However, the PJM Transmission Owners recognize that PJM’s combined study approach will consider impacts associated with generator interconnection requests, and thus, a contribution from generators to offset the costs of IRRs is appropriate,” the transmission owners explained.
Securing Transmission Revenues. The PJM transmission owners’ proposed Cost Recovery Agreement (CRA) would establish minimum recurring revenue commitments ranging from 80% to 100% of the revenues associated with the customer’s requested firm transmission service. Customers would pay the difference between the required contribution and qualifying revenues from transmission service actually taken. Credit support would be based on 100% of the projected full-service revenue benchmark for the remaining commitment period.
MISO proposes a different revenue guarantee. Under its Large Load Cost Recovery Agreement, where the costs of covered network upgrades are rolled into transmission rates, customers would assume financial commitments designed to recover the return on and of those investments over 20 years, including depreciation, operations and maintenance expenses, and taxes. MISO illustrates the mechanism using a $10 million annual revenue commitment: if attributable transmission service revenues total $7 million during a calendar year, the customer would owe a $3 million supplemental payment. No supplemental payment would be required if revenues meet or exceed the commitment.
ISO-NE’s participating transmission owners, meanwhile, propose a three-party Large Load Cost Recovery Agreement that would directly involve the entity developing the large-load facility. The entity would reimburse the interconnecting transmission owner for directly assigned facilities and pay applicable charges to offset revenue requirements for qualifying network upgrades. Early termination or disconnection would trigger an exit fee based on the remaining net book value of covered upgrades. The New England Power Pool (NEPOOL), notably, did not join the filing with respect to the proposed cost recovery agreement.
Pricing Interruptible Access. PJM’s transmission owners also propose to establish a maximum rate for non-firm contract demand transmission service based on the corresponding zonal firm rate and the transmission system’s load factor in that zone. In one illustrative calculation, a firm rate of $90,000/MW-year and a load factor of approximately 64.7% would produce an annualized maximum non-firm rate of $58,219/MW-year—a 35.3% discount. MISO has yet to propose specific transmission rates for GRITS.
NYISO’s proposed System Reliability Benefit Fee would address a separate issue: the capacity market benefits received by large loads that do not secure firm withdrawal rights. The charge would be assessed to load-serving entities based on the authorized quantities of non-firm or zero withdrawal service in MW, not actual energy withdrawals in MWh.
Behind-the-Meter Generation Netting. PJM proposes to limit the daily demand reduction attributable to retail behind-the-meter generation to 50 MW at a single electrical location for purposes of calculating applicable transmission charges and capacity obligations. The proposal includes transitional provisions for existing installations, protections for qualifying contractual arrangements, and exemptions for certain cogeneration facilities whose loads follow the generation offline if the generating facility trips.
ISO-NE proposes a zero-megawatt netting threshold for large loads for wholesale service settlements. NYISO proposes to discontinue its existing Behind-the-Meter Net Generation Resource participation model, which has only six active resources, by May 1, 2029. Its proposed large-load rules would assess several reliability-related service charges, including operating reserves, black start, voltage support, and regulation, on gross demand.
MISO would similarly assess regulation and black start charges on gross demand under GRITS. CAISO, by contrast, proposes to preserve its existing methodology for calculating transmission access charges, which allows certain onsite generation and storage output to offset facility demand, but would require gross-demand billing for regulation and black start services at large loads served by co-located generation.

A Multiyear Implementation Effort
The timelines for the proposed reforms extend well beyond FERC’s consideration of the November filings. Most of PJM’s transmission service revisions would take effect March 16, 2027, under its requested schedule, but the Fast Energization Process and associated reinforcement cost allocation methodology would commence after its existing interconnection cycle completes its second decision point, which PJM expects in late November 2027.
ISO-NE proposes to begin accepting applications under its new study procedures on June 1, 2027, and offer its new transmission services beginning June 1, 2028. NYISO’s Large Load Integration Procedures would take effect Feb. 1, 2027, ahead of most of its associated market participation revisions on June 1, 2028. CAISO has requested a Feb. 16, 2027, effective date for most reforms, though associated settlement revisions would become effective April 30, 2028. MISO does not anticipate implementing GRITS before Jan. 1, 2029, owing to the required software modifications.

retained_collection_events.source_quote: Five U.S. regional grid operators have submitted sweeping tariff reforms to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) that could fundamentally change how data centers and other large electricity consumers connect to the transmission system, secure access to generating capacity, and pay for the necessary infrastructure.

The proposals, filed Nov. 13 and 16 in response to FERC’s June 18 show-cause orders , mark a broad effort, seeking to accelerate large-load energization without compromising grid reliability or shifting the costs of new infrastructure to existing customers.

The California Independent System Operator (CAISO) , by contrast, argues that a customer-specific generation procurement requirement is unnecessary under its existing resource adequacy framework and has proposed a Flexible Interim Load Interconnection (FILI) arrangement to accommodate earlier energization subject to transmission constraints.

The November filings stem from six proceedings FERC initiated June 18 under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act (FPA), after the Commission preliminarily found that existing regional transmission tariffs may be unjust and unreasonable or unduly discriminatory or preferential in their treatment of large loads.

The orders identified five broad areas for reform: efficient transmission service studies, rules for co-located loads and loads served by behind-the-meter generation, transmission services for flexible loads, studies of generating facilities serving electrically proximate large loads and co-located loads, and transparency in infrastructure costs and cost allocation.

The Commission provided an avenue for each regional transmission organization (RTO) and independent system operator (ISO) to propose tariff revisions tailored to its existing transmission, market, and regulatory framework under Section 205 of the FPA.

On Aug. 14, the Commission granted requests to hold the show-cause proceedings in abeyance to accommodate those filings, establishing response deadlines of Nov. 16 for five grid operators and Nov. 20 for Southwest Power Pool (SPP) .
The Commission first advanced new transmission service options for co-located loads in PJM before proposing their broader application across all six jurisdictional regional grid operators.

The June orders also advance objectives outlined in an Oct. 23, 2025, directive from Energy Secretary Chris Wright , who invoked Section 403 of the Department of Energy (DOE) Organization Act to initiate rulemaking procedures on large-load interconnection to the interstate transmission system.
“The tailored show cause orders encourage each RTO/ISO to work with its transmission owners and stakeholders to address the challenges to timely interconnect large loads.

For example, in contrast to a rulemaking that would propose uniform national standards, the show cause orders allow FERC to recognize different paths to progress in this area, such as the tariff progress already made by the PJM Interconnection, LLC (PJM) and SPP regions,” FERC’s Office of Public Participation explained in guidance updated Oct. 19 .
The proposed tariffs address both constraints through different combinations of transmission service rights, mandatory curtailment, and capacity procurement obligations.
The load would remain subject to existing capacity procurement requirements throughout the transition.
Historical market data suggest that the threshold would permit service in more than 95% of hours, MISO said.

Under NYISO’s existing Constraint Specific Shortage Pricing mechanism, a six-step transmission demand curve produces a constraint price of $4,000/MWh at full utilization of a transmission facility’s Constraint Reliability Margin.

Because CAISO does not administer a centralized forward capacity market, responsibility for procuring adequate resources rests principally on load-serving entities (LSEs) under requirements established by the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) and other applicable local regulatory authorities.
The absence of a customer-specific generation requirement therefore does not eliminate advance capacity procurement obligations or guarantee immediate service at every location.”

CAISO acknowledged that the effectiveness of its framework depends on timely resource procurement and development and that large loads could materialize faster than existing forecasts and procurement processes anticipate.

NioBay Metals President and CEO Jean-Sébastien David (L) chats with TNM Western Editor Henry Lazenby in Montreal.
Posted By: Henry Lazenby November 19, 2026
NioBay Metals (TSXV: NBY; US-OTC: NBYCF) plans to test material from its Crevier project in Quebec at more than 10 times the scale of its first pilot run as it seeks buyers for high-purity niobium and tantalum oxides.
A bulk sample from Crevier, about 320 km north of Quebec City, has been crushed and bagged and is waiting for a slot at a test facility. Earlier tests yielded niobium oxide at about 99.6% purity and tantalum oxide at 99.98%.
“So, with that, we will be able to produce more material for more clients,” President and CEO Jean-Sébastien David told The Northern Miner in Montreal early this month. “Because for now, we have nothing left, so we need to produce, produce and produce.”
An earlier plan for Crevier called for ferroniobium for steelmakers. NioBay is now targeting markets such as batteries, where buyers can take a year to qualify the material, David said.

Kia’s EV lineup covers just about every size and price point, but it believes one thing is still missing: a truly cheap electric car. That’s about to change in 2027, when Kia plans to unveil a new EV that could start at around $22,000 to $24,000.
Is Kia launching the EV1 in 2027?
It’s been 40 years since Kia introduced its first electric vehicle, the Besta EV , created so runners in the 1986 Asian Games wouldn’t have to breathe toxic fumes from the broadcast vehicle.
Kia has come a long way since the Besta EV hit the road, now offering a complete lineup of electric vehicles, from compact SUVs and hatchbacks to vans and three-row SUVs.
In Europe and the UK, Kia’s electric lineup consists of the EV2, EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, EV9, and PV5 van, but the Korean automaker isn’t done yet.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
“With no intention of resting on its laurels,” Kia said, the brand plans to complete development of its first software-defined vehicle (SDV) by the end of 2027, an all-new B-segment EV hatchback.
It didn’t offer any other details on the upcoming EV, but Ted Lee, Kia’s executive vice president and head of global operations, told Auto Express that Kia and Hyundai are co-developing a new dedicated EV architecture for an upcoming pair of entry-level electric cars.
Kia reveals plans to launch its first software-defined electric vehicle (Source: Kia)
Expected to arrive as the Hyundai IONIQ 1 and Kia EV1, the new EVs will compete with other entry-level electric cars like the Renault Twingo, which starts at about €20,000.
Lee said the EV1’s price will be highly competitive not just with other entry-level EVs, but also with small gas-powered cars, with prices expected to start in the €20,000 to €22,000 range, or about $22,000 to $24,000. And that’s without government incentives.
Kia EV2 First Edition (Source: Kia UK)
The EV2 starts at just €26,600 ($29,500) in Germany and other European markets as Kia’s current entry-level EV, so the price range would make sense.
While it will be Kia’s cheapest EV, Lee promised it would not cut corners in quality, design, or features.
Kia reveals plans to launch its first software-defined electric vehicle (Source: Kia)
As its first SDV, the EV1 will feature Kia and Hyundai Motor’s latest-generation tech and software. Kia said the electric SDV will offer Level 2+ autonomous driving on highways. In 2029, Kia plans to expand to Level 2++, enabling it to operate in cities.
The new EV will also use Hyundai’s SDV architecture (CODA), the Pleos Connect infotainment system, and Gleo AI, an in-vehicle Agenic AI.
The Kia Vision Meta Turismo EV concept (Source: Kia)

Posted By: Henry Lazenby November 19, 2026
Spartan Metals (TSXV: W; US-OTC: SPRMF) estimates it would cost $683 million (C$978 million) to build an underground tungsten and molybdenum mine at Victorio in New Mexico, with a plant to turn tungsten concentrate into a feedstock for cutting tools and other industrial products.
The project, about 440 km southwest of state capital Santa Fe, would operate for 24 years, according to a preliminary economic assessment released Thursday. The study estimates an after-tax net present value (NPV) of $2.14 billion, at an 8% discount rate, and a 31% internal rate of return. The project requires another $2.03 billion in spending to sustain the operation over its life.
“Both metals contribute to those economics, so continued price appreciation for either metal can make a meaningful difference to the underlying project economics,” Spartan CEO Brett Marsh said in the release. “Victorio could become a lasting domestic source of tungsten and molybdenum for U.S. industrial and defense customers.”
The United States last mined tungsten commercially in 2015, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. China accounts for about 85% of global capacity to refine ammonium paratungstate, the intermediate product Victorio would make, according to S&P Global. China’s export controls are keeping supply tight even as some buyers balk at elevated prices, Fastmarkets reported Thursday.
Spartan shares closed unchanged at C26¢ apiece on Thursday in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$15.4 million ($10.7 million).
Price sensitivity
The study assumes $1,350 per 10 kg of tungsten trioxide and $20 per lb. of molybdenum. At the lowest prices tested, $750 per 10 kg for tungsten trioxide and $15 per lb. for molybdenum, the after-tax NPV falls to $392 million and the return to 14%.
Victorio would use block caving, an underground method that uses gravity to break the rock. The study projects annual recovery of about 4,100 tonnes of tungsten trioxide contained in ammonium paratungstate and 8.65 million lb. of molybdenum in concentrate. Inferred resources account for 39% of scheduled plant feed.
An August resource estimate puts measured and indicated resources at 76.7 million tonnes grading 0.1% tungsten trioxide and 0.09% molybdenum, containing 165.5 million lb. and 147.9 million lb., respectively. Another 92.4 million inferred tonnes grade 0.09% tungsten trioxide and 0.06% molybdenum, for 187.6 million lb. and 130 million lb., respectively.
Next steps
Spartan plans to advance Victorio to prefeasibility. The study recommends $13.2 million of work, including drilling, metallurgical testing and studies of water supply and tailings. Spartan has an option on the core claims from Donegan Resources. Exercising it requires cash payments, $14 million in exploration spending and a feasibility study by 2034 under a March agreement.
Other tungsten projects are advancing elsewhere in North America. Canada’s federal government on Monday conditionally approved up to C$14 million in financing for Fireweed Metals (TSX: FWZ; US-OTC: FWEDF) to help advance its Mactung tungsten project toward a construction decision.

source_document.body:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has offered up to $2.8 billion in conditional financing for Wyoming Intertie, a proposed 106-mile transmission project in southeastern Wyoming that could more than double existing power transfer capacity between the Eastern and Western Interconnections, the nation’s two largest synchronous grids. The federal loan, which could be assigned to utilities that acquire capacity on the line, would finance the majority of the independently developed project’s construction costs.
The DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) announced the conditional commitment on Nov. 17 for the up-to-1,800-MW project, under development by Houston-based independent transmission company Grid United. The project would expand transfer capability between the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) and Western Electricity Coordinating Council (WECC) regions.
Existing transfer capacity between the Eastern and Western Interconnections totals just 1,320 MW, according to Grid United’s October 2026 open house materials . The DOE estimates Wyoming Intertie could yield up to $39 billion in electricity cost savings across 17 states in the WECC and SPP regions, though the department did not detail the methodology underlying that projection in its announcement.
According to Grid United’s October financing fact sheet , the proposed loan would cover 80% of construction costs over a 30-year term that includes the construction period. The $2.8 billion excludes interest during construction. Loan disbursements would begin only after the project receives notice to proceed and enters construction.
Grid United separately estimates that the lower federal borrowing rate would yield more than $500 million in ratepayer savings compared with private market project financing. The company notes that the federal loan could be assigned to utilities that acquire capacity on the transmission line.
The DOE said the commitment advances President Donald Trump’s executive order “Strengthening the Reliability and Security of the U.S. Electric Grid” and builds on the department’s September project selections under the Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Advanced Transmission Technology Upgrades (SPARK) program.
Expanding Transfer Capacity Between Asynchronous Grids
The Eastern and Western Interconnections operate as separate, asynchronous alternating current (AC) systems that cannot exchange power directly over conventional AC transmission ties. Seven existing back-to-back high-voltage direct current (HVDC) converter facilities enable power transfers between the two interconnections, Grid United noted in Feb. 25, 2025, comments to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) on the North American Electric Reliability Corp.’s (NERC’s) Interregional Transfer Capability Study. The existing facilities are distributed across Montana, South Dakota, Nebraska, Colorado, and New Mexico, with individual ratings of 130 MW to 210 MW. Five date to between 1977 and 1988 and employ older line-commutated converter (LCC) technology.
Wyoming Intertie would connect the existing Aeolus substation near Medicine Bow in the Western Interconnection to a proposed HVDC back-to-back converter station near the Laramie River Station outside Wheatland. The transmission route extends through Wyoming’s Carbon, Albany, and Platte counties.
Documents suggest the converter station would employ voltage source converter (VSC) technology. In a back-to-back configuration, incoming AC power is converted to direct current (DC) and then back to AC at a single site, which allows power exchanges between grids without synchronization. According to Grid United’s financing fact sheet, the VSC equipment would provide rapid control of bidirectional power flows, voltage regulation, and support for black-start restoration. The latter capability could allow an energized grid to assist in the restoration of portions of the neighboring system after a major outage.
“As a networked grid infrastructure asset, Wyoming Intertie will not directly connect to any specific generation or demand source,” Grid United notes in its project materials . The line would accommodate power from all generation technologies and allow transfers in either direction according to real-time demand.
The additional capacity could allow grid operators to access surplus generation in one interconnection during supply shortages in the other, particularly during extreme weather events. Grid United also anticipates that geographic and meteorological diversity across the two systems, along with differences in their generation profiles, would allow utilities to import electricity during periods of lower production costs and provide Wyoming generators access to additional markets.
Grid United’s proposed 106-mile Wyoming Intertie would connect the existing Aeolus substation near Medicine Bow to a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) back-to-back converter station near the Laramie River Station outside Wheatland, Wyoming. The project would provide up to 1,800 MW of bidirectional power transfer capacity between the Eastern and Western Interconnections. Courtesy: Grid United
Commercial Development and Regulatory Approvals
Still, the federal financing commitment arrives relatively early in Wyoming Intertie’s development. Grid United has not publicly identified capacity customers in its announcement materials, though its financing fact sheet identifies commercial capacity contracts, acquisition of the full project right-of-way, receipt of federal, state, and local permits, and compliance with federal program requirements as key conditions of financial close.
The DOE’s conditional commitment also requires the project to satisfy technical, legal, environmental, and financial conditions before the department executes definitive financing agreements.
Grid United began field surveys in 2023, initiated acquisition of right-of-way options in 2024, and entered the federal Coordinated Interagency Transmission Authorizations and Permits (CITAP) process in 2025, according to its October 2026 development schedule .
Portions of the proposed route cross federally owned land and require environmental reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). At the state level, the project requires an Industrial Siting Certificate through the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality. Carbon and Platte counties also require conditional use permits, though Albany County currently does not, according to Grid United’s October open house materials.
The developer anticipates concurrent state and county permitting processes in 2027 and 2028, followed by issuance of a federal environmental record of decision and a permitting notice to proceed in 2029. Construction of the transmission line and converter station could begin as early as 2030. Grid United projects commercial operation in 2032 or 2033, subject to HVDC equipment procurement.
Grid United’s October project overview notes that route development incorporates input from landowners, Tribal Nations, and local communities, and the alignment remains subject to regulatory approval. The project has also established a community investment program in partnership with the Wyoming Community Foundation. As of October 2026, the program had awarded $1.2 million to 73 organizations across the three host counties, with local community committees responsible for grant recipient selection.
Grid United’s October 2026 development schedule for Wyoming Intertie anticipates completion of federal environmental reviews and issuance of a permitting notice to proceed in 2029. Construction of the transmission line and converter station could begin as early as 2030, with commercial operation projected for 2032 or 2033, contingent on high-voltage direct current (HVDC) equipment procurement. Courtesy: Grid United
Grid United’s Interregional Transmission Portfolio
Grid United is developing a portfolio of five major transmission projects across the central and western U.S. Along with Wyoming Intertie, the portfolio includes North Plains Connector, Three Corners Connector, Pecos West, and Southline Transmission Project. Several of the projects have secured federal support through programs established under the previous administration or advanced under the DOE’s more recent transmission initiatives.
The 3,000-MW North Plains Connector is an approximately 420-mile HVDC transmission line rated at up to 525 kV between Montana and North Dakota that would connect the Western Interconnection to the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) and SPP regions. In August 2024, the DOE selected the Montana Department of Commerce for up to $700 million in funding under the Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships (GRIP) program, established by the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. The award supports North Plains Connector and upgrades to the existing Colstrip transmission system. On Oct. 22, 2026, the North Plains Connector Utility Consortium confirmed finalization of the GRIP award at approximately $695 million. Of that amount, the transmission project will receive approximately $620 million as a subrecipient to the Montana Department of Commerce, primarily for transmission tower engineering and construction. The DOE and the Montana Department of Environmental Quality issued the project’s final environmental impact statement on Aug. 28, 2026.
Grid United’s 1,800-MW Three Corners Connector, a proposed 300-mile HVDC line rated at up to 525 kV, would connect the existing transmission systems near Pueblo, Colorado, and Guymon, Oklahoma. In September 2026, the DOE selected an application from Oklahoma’s Office of Management and Enterprise Services for negotiations under the SPARK program. The application seeks up to $250 million in federal funding, primarily for transmission tower engineering and materials. According to an Oct. 7 project announcement , the funding remains contingent on execution of a formal financial assistance agreement. Three Corners Connector could enter commercial operation as early as 2031.
North Plains Connector, Three Corners Connector, and Wyoming Intertie would all incorporate VSC technology, according to Grid United’s February 2025 FERC filing. Their combined proposed project ratings total 6,600 MW—five times the existing East-West transfer capability.
Grid United’s southwestern development portfolio includes Pecos West, a proposed HVDC project that would link El Paso, Texas, and southeastern New Mexico, and Southline, an approximately 280-mile, double-circuit, high-voltage transmission project that Grid United is co-developing with Black Forest Partners between New Mexico and Arizona.
Southline has secured federal support through a separate mechanism. The DOE selected the project’s first phase in 2023 and its second phase in 2024 for capacity contracts under the $2.5 billion Transmission Facilitation Program . Under the program, the DOE can contract for transmission capacity to help developers establish the commercial commitments necessary to advance construction. Payment for transmission service under such contracts does not begin until the infrastructure is operational and available to provide service.
Financing Independent Transmission Development
Grid United has previously identified limitations in existing transmission planning procedures that could complicate commercial development of interregional projects. In its February 2025 FERC comments , the company urged the commission to establish a framework under Order 1920, its long-term regional transmission planning and cost allocation rule, to explicitly evaluate the reliability benefits of interregional transmission investments.
“Additionally, many regions count this value operationally, but none that Grid United can find puts value on it proactively or for new lines,” the company wrote. Grid United argued that the omission reduces the assessed value of prospective interregional transmission investments and makes participant-funded projects more difficult to develop.
EDF’s Wyoming Intertie commitment represents a different application of federal financing from either infrastructure grants or capacity contracts. The office, formerly the DOE’s Loan Programs Office, has more than $289 billion in available loan authority and has concentrated its recent financing activity on baseload generation, transmission, and nuclear power projects, as POWER has reported .
In July 2026, EDF closed a $3.26 billion loan to AEP Texas for approximately 100 transmission projects that encompass roughly 2,800 miles of lines. In October 2026, the office closed a $5.1 billion financing package for Alliant Energy’s utilities in Iowa and Wisconsin.
While those transactions involved regulated utilities with established mechanisms for infrastructure cost recovery, EDF’s Wyoming Intertie commitment precedes fulfillment of the independent project’s commercial contracting requirements. The potential assignment of the federal loan to utilities that acquire transmission capacity could improve the economics of those agreements before construction begins.
The announcement follows EDF’s $4.2 billion conditional commitment to Vistra for nuclear power uprates in Ohio and Pennsylvania and its conditional commitment of up to $5 billion to Constellation for uprates at eight nuclear plants.

source_document.body:
Anyone who has managed drivers knows that communication is rarely clean, even in the best of times. In a post-Montgomery liability environment, a late load, a tired driver or a casual text can become evidence. For freight brokers, whose business runs on relationships and fast decisions, the question is how to stay responsive without creating legal exposure.
That question is now landing on the desks of chief legal officers at some of the industry’s largest brokerages. At the FreightWaves Brokerage Compliance Symposium at F3, Aqil Naeem, co-founder and CEO of E3 Group , described how those conversations shaped the company’s products. E3 has built what Naeem describes as the biggest driver verification platform, and now one of the biggest driver communication platforms.
“These conversations stem from our conversations with many of the chief legal officers at the many top 20 brokers that we work with,” Naeem said. Those legal leaders came to E3 with an open question about how to handle driver communication when a single slip could carry exposure in the hundreds of millions. It became a core product issue and a standing topic with every customer: “how should you be talking to drivers in a safe way that doesn’t lead to a lawsuit.”
Where Courts Draw the Line
The risk doesn’t come from routine contact. According to Naeem, courts focus on a narrower question of whether a broker’s language shaped what the driver did.
“What courts really focus on are not people doing regular check-ins, etc. They have this doctrine about exercising agency over the driver,” Naeem said. Asking whether a driver is on track is one thing. Adding a reference to a $10,000 or $15,000 fine is another, even when the fine is accurate. “By mentioning a fine to someone, for example, even though it may be factual, that is a greater indication of exercising agency over what that driver is doing.”
The same logic applies on the verification side. Naeem pointed to a court case in which a broker was found liable for failing to verify that its carrier hadn’t double brokered the freight. Because the broker hadn’t done a simple check that the person picking up the load was who it should have been, it was held responsible.
His conclusion: “It really comes down to how extensive your SOPs are and gearing your SOPs around doing your minimum job as a freight broker, i.e., validating who’s picking it up, making sure they’re on time, and communicating what’s happening with that load, as opposed to exercising too much control over that load.”
Two Camps, No Consensus
Brokers have responded in very different ways. Naeem sees two ends of the spectrum. Some brokers want little to no contact with drivers, and some E3 customers have asked to hide data in the verification product to limit what they can see. At the other end are brokers with long SOPs designed to catch every contingency. “A lot of them are ironically going to these like 20 question SOPs,” he said, with every driver contact turning into a health and safety checklist.
Neither approach settles the hardest scenarios. If a driver reports being sick and the broker escalates to the dispatcher, who then fails to replace the driver, could a court find the broker negligent for not sourcing another carrier with eight hours of lead time? Naeem noted that opinions in court tend to run against brokers, because a broker looks like a large company with deep pockets rather than a business operating on thin margins.
His assessment was candid: “there is no right answer in terms of how you should be handling things it’s really just a function of becoming aware of them.”
Operations teams face a related dilemma when a driver says they’re low on hours or too tired to make delivery. Asking about a backup driver could be read as pressure to keep driving. Resetting the appointment and absorbing the customer fallout carries its own cost. “You just have to pick the kind of poison that you’re willing to live with,” Naeem said, adding that the right call may vary by customer, since some have stricter delivery requirements than others.
Low-Hanging Fruit: The Rate Confirmation
While the gray areas stay open, Naeem sees some fixes as straightforward. The first is the rate confirmation. He described cases in which brokers were sued after shippers added fines to the rate confirmation and the broker delivered that document to the driver. The argument was that the broker, by passing along the penalty, had exercised agency over the driver and pressured the driver to arrive on time.
“Step one has to be auditing what you put on the rate confirmation,” Naeem said. “The rate confirmation is your very first audited document that you are giving to the carrier and the driver, and so ensuring that you strip that of any potential language that might cause adverse behavior, I think is step number one.”
The second step is defining what happens after pickup, including how late loads are documented and how questions and exceptions are escalated.
Automating the Routine, Escalating the Exception
Naeem sees the most technologically advanced brokers moving toward automated communication governed by a documented SOP. Part of the appeal is legal. He described brokers who want to adopt a state-of-the-art system and a detailed SOP, then point to that when something goes wrong. “They want to take responsibility over the SOPs. They do not want to be responsible for the individual to individual communication.”
His guidance is to separate the load lifecycle into stages. Before pickup, brokers should minimize operational burden and automate standard checks, especially confirming that the person arriving at the dock actually works for the assigned carrier. By his estimate, about a third of the brokers he talks with don’t do that today, and the two-thirds who do it manually “open themselves up to even more liability.”
After pickup, he recommends more care. “I.e., a driver is on time, everything checks out with that load. You maybe don’t want someone talking to that person, right? You might want to have it purely automated and let things go.” If the driver replies that something is wrong, the conversation escalates to a human. “I think you’re not going to have a fully agentic solution to this, but I think having agents as a first line of defense to start auditing everything and injecting this information is also really important.”
Call Recording and the Records Problem
On call recording, Naeem has seen both extremes. Some brokers record every call on their VoIP platform and others record none. Selective recording is the approach he cautioned against, saying that choosing not to record conversations with carriers “also looks bad in the court.” His broader point: “ignoring the problem is not the solution.” Any driver can claim a broker said something, he noted, and without a record the broker has little way to respond .
Retention raises its own concerns. Naeem deferred to legal counsel on how long to keep communications, describing his approach as asking chief legal officers how much appetite they have, since more data can support performance analysis. For personally identifiable information, though, his advice was firm: “whenever you’re dealing with PII, you want that destroyed immediately.” He said he has met top 50 brokers with tens of thousands of driver CDLs sitting in email that haven’t been destroyed, each one a hefty potential fine if not destroyed after permitted use.
E3’s approach is to store hashes of driver identities instead of the documents themselves. With about 7,000 drivers verified per day and more than half a million owner-operators seen, Naeem said, the network can recognize a returning driver without the broker collecting a CDL. He also expects some brokers to sunset internal projects that track historical communication data for proprietary on-time metrics, because of the risk of holding records that are incomplete when an incident occurs.
The Shipper Pressure Point
Looking ahead, Naeem sees liability exposure moving up the supply chain. Shippers are paying closer attention to whether their brokers have verification and communication controls in place. He cited the Unilever lawsuit, in which no one checked that the truck arriving at the facility belonged to the intended carrier. After an incident, the shipper became a defendant and, in his words, views the case as a brand risk.
For brokers, he sees an opening rather than a blanket threat. “The brokers who are able to solve this problem, come up with a great solution, are going to have an edge in the market because they’re going to be able to show shippers that hey, I have I have our ship under control,” he said. “I actually think it’s an opportunity for brokers who are active about it.”
No single playbook has emerged on escalation, repowering decisions or AI after pickup, and brokers are making these calls with competing legal and operational risks on both sides. Auditing rate confirmations, tightening SOPs, verifying pickups and minimizing sensitive data are steps within a broker’s control today, and shippers are starting to ask which brokers have taken them.

2027 Genesis G80 and GV80 Get Hybrid Powertrain Option With 347 HP and Liquid-Cooled Battery
7 photos
Photo: Genesis
Genesis debuted its first hybrid powertrain on the 2027 G80 and GV80. This builds on the strengths of the trusted 2.5-liter gasoline engine by adding an electric motor and the first liquid-cooled battery in a Hyundai Motor Group's hybrid system. The new powertrain develops 347 horsepower and promises over 500 miles of range on a full tank.
Hybrids are the new gold for carmakers operating in North America, and Genesis has a strong reason to offer them. The luxury brand owned by the Hyundai Motor Group has tried to push electric mobility into the upper echelon of the US market. However, the move has backfired, and Genesis had to axe the all-electric G80 Electrified in 2025 due to low sales, while the GV70 Electrified is barely hanging on.
The Los Angeles Motor Show marks the debut of the brand's first hybrid powertrain on the G80 sedan and GV80 SUV , and it's full of surprises. Less so in the engine compartment, where you'll still find the trusted 2.5-liter gasoline engine . However, the electrified part introduces interesting solutions that show Genesis has put some effort into this hybrid powerplant.
First, there's a starter-generator motor on the combustion engine, which basically turns it into a mild hybrid. Then there's the drive motor, which can directly drive the rear wheels without the help of the gas engine. Genesis doesn't offer more technical details except that this is a parallel hybrid system, but what comes next is even more intriguing.
Genesis announced that the hybrid system is powered by Hyundai Motor Group's first liquid-cooled battery installed on a hybrid vehicle. The carmaker mentions benefits such as better thermal management, enabling deeper discharge and more power output. This will allow Genesis to cycle the battery more aggressively without affecting its longevity.
Photo: Genesis There's no word on how much capacity the battery pack has, what the power of the drive motor is, and how far the G80/GV80 can drive in EV Mode. However, to add to the confusion, Genesis states that both the G80 and GV80 have an estimated range of more than 500 miles (805 km). Range is not a usual specification for gas or hybrid vehicles, whose efficiency is measured in miles per gallon. Instead, range is a more adequate metric for electric vehicles.
The choice of words, as well as the liquid-cooled battery, would make more sense in a plug-in hybrid, but that's not what Genesis communicated about the G80 HEV and GV80 HEV . However, I wouldn't rule out a longer all-electric range than on mundane hybrid vehicles, which usually can't go more than a mile in EV mode.
Genesis appears to support this theory by fitting the new hybrid powertrain with some auxiliary components that ensure cabin comfort even when the combustion engine is stopped. For instance, the two hybrid models offer Stay Mode, which allows climate control and multimedia functions to operate without starting the engine. Genesis also says that the electric motor engages on a broader range of driving conditions to create a driving experience "closer to that of an EV."
